analysis.one_liner: Bars cities and counties from regulating the sale or use of pesticides.
analysis.headline: The bill would have stopped cities and counties from regulating pesticide use, but it never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal pesticide law to say that no city, county, town, or other local government can make or keep any rule about how pesticides are sold, labeled, or applied. States and the EPA would remain the only levels of government allowed to regulate pesticides. It was introduced by Representative Rodney Davis and 16 Republican cosponsors and was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Pesticide manufacturers and commercial applicators would gain, because they would face one set of state and federal rules instead of stricter local ordinances on top of them. Growers and pesticide users would also face fewer overlapping rules. The bill's original cosponsors were all Republicans, several from agricultural districts.

how_it_helps.text: It amends federal pesticide law to add that a 'political subdivision of a State' cannot impose or keep any requirement on the sale, distribution, labeling, application, or use of pesticides covered by state or EPA rules.
This would apply nationwide, preventing towns and counties from acting even where local officials want stricter rules than their state allows.

analysis.who_pays: Residents and local governments would pay: communities that want tighter restrictions on spraying in parks, near schools, or around homes would lose the ability to act, even if their state has not acted. Existing local pesticide rules could be wiped out.

drawbacks.text: By barring local rules on pesticide sale and use, the bill would strip the level of government closest to residents of any power to restrict spraying in parks, near schools, or around homes, even where local officials believe federal and state rules are too lax.
The prohibition is retroactive in effect: it says localities shall not 'continue in effect' any existing pesticide requirement, meaning rules communities already adopted could be wiped out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is uniform statewide rules that spare pesticide users from navigating a patchwork of town ordinances. The cost is that it strips residents of the government level closest to them—city and county councils—as a way to restrict pesticide spraying around homes, schools, and parks, and it would void protections local governments had already put in place. Weighing those, the bill's main effect is to remove a check on pesticide use, and it died before any trade-off was tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Agriculture Committee and its subcommittee from April 2022 until Congress ended in January 2023, never getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: It was introduced on March 29, 2022 and referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the same day.
On April 18, 2022 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Biotechnology, Horticulture, and Research, where it stayed.
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Local governments keep their authority, since the preemption never became law. Pesticide makers and commercial users gained nothing because the bill died, but they lose nothing either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Local governments keep their pesticide authority

for.name: Rep. Rodney Davis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit local pesticide regulation.

for.name: 16 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all of them Republicans.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats signed on, and the bill never advanced beyond referral.

industries.note: The bill would lock in a single federal-state regulatory framework and eliminate stricter local rules, protecting sales of products that cities or counties might otherwise restrict or ban. Local preemption of this kind has long been a priority for pesticide makers.

Applicators and growers would face one uniform set of rules instead of differing local ordinances. The cost falls on residents who lose the ability to set local conditions for spraying near homes, schools, and parks.

Cities, counties, and towns would lose all authority over pesticide use within their borders, including any rules already in place, under the bill's 'shall not impose, or continue in effect' language.
